units.Ezra 3:1: The seventh month arrived—the sons of Israel being in their cities—and the people gathered as one man in Jerusalem.
units.Ezra 3:2: Iesous son of Iosedek and his brothers the priests, and Zorobabel son of Salathiel and his brothers, arose and built the altar of the God of Israel, to offer whole burnt offerings upon it according to what is written in the law of Moses, the man of God.
units.Ezra 3:3: They prepared the altar on its prepared place, for terror from the peoples of the lands was upon them. A whole burnt offering went up upon it to the Lord, in the morning and toward evening.
units.Ezra 3:4: They kept the Festival of Booths according to what was written, with whole burnt offerings day by day in the number required by the ordinance, each day’s due on its own day,
units.Ezra 3:5: and afterward continual whole burnt offerings, those for the new moons and all the consecrated festivals, and for everyone freely presenting a freewill offering to the Lord.
units.Ezra 3:7: They gave silver to the stonecutters and craftsmen, and food, drink and oil to the Sedanin and Sorin, to bring cedar timber from Lebanon to the sea at Joppa, according to the concession of Cyrus king of the Persians to them.
units.Ezra 3:8: In the second year after their arrival at the house of God in Jerusalem, in the second month, Zorobabel son of Salathiel, Iesous son of Iosedek, the rest of their brothers the priests and Levites, and all who had come from captivity to Jerusalem began. units.Ezra 3:9: Iesous and his sons and his brothers, Kadmiel and his sons, sons of Judah, stood over those doing the work in the house of God; also the sons of Enadad, their sons and their brothers the Levites.
units.Ezra 3:10: They laid the foundation for building the Lord’s house, and the priests stood in their vestments with trumpets, and the Levites, sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the Lord according to the directions of David king of Israel.
units.Ezra 3:11: They answered in praise and thanksgiving to the Lord: “For it is good, for His mercy toward Israel endures for ever.” All the people sounded a great cry of praise to the Lord at the founding of the Lord’s house.
units.Ezra 3:12: Many of the priests and Levites and leaders of the families—the elders who had seen the first house at its founding, and who saw this house before their eyes—wept with a loud voice; and the multitude cried aloud with joy to raise a song.

units.Esther 7:5: The king said, “Who is this who dared to do this deed?”
units.Esther 7:6: Esther said, “An enemy—this wicked Haman!” Haman was disturbed before the king and the queen.

reread_versions.rationale: The narrator separates the resumption of whole burnt offerings on the first day of the seventh month, while the house remained unfounded, from the second-year building work and foundation ceremony. The later dated scene supplies the next stage of the restoration; sacrificial worship had resumed before that construction milestone.

reread_versions.rationale: Both Jerusalem restoration celebrations produce a sound heard far away. Ezra describes an indistinguishable mixture of joyful cries and weeping at the temple foundation, whereas the wall-dedication context in Nehemiah presents the gladness of the people, wives and children. The shared far-reaching celebration does not erase Ezra's sorrow or equate the ceremonies.

reread_versions.rationale: Ezra expressly identifies a royal document as written in Syrian and interpreted; Daniel expressly identifies the Chaldeans' address to the king as spoken in the Syrian language. The connection is the texts' own naming of the language in royal communication, with written correspondence distinguished from spoken audience; it does not identify the rulers or documents.

reread_versions.rationale: Darius's decree prescribes fastening a violator to timber taken from his own house. In Esther the king orders Haman fastened to the tree erected at Haman's place for Mordecai. Both punishments use wood associated with the offender's own premises; one is a prospective sanction against changing the decree, the other the narrated reversal of Haman's prepared execution. Neither is asserted to be an enforcement of the other.

reread_versions.relationship: institutional comparison of priestly fiscal privilege
reread_versions.rationale: Ezra exempts the personnel serving God's house from taxation and enslavement. Genesis distinguishes the Egyptian priests' land, supported by Pharaoh's allowance and not bought by him, from the land subject to the fifth. Both texts reserve a fiscal privilege connected with priestly service, but Ezra's protected workers and Egypt's exempt land are different provisions in different religious settings.

reread_versions.rationale: Arthasastha's decree protects temple servants from taxation; Demetrius's letter offers tax remissions to the Jews and declares Jerusalem and its territory holy and exempt from tithes and dues. Both royal texts connect fiscal exemption with Jerusalem's sacred community, with Ezra naming service personnel and the letter naming the city and territory. The latter remains an offer that Jonathan and the people reject in 10:46, not proof that the exemption took effect.
